findings.summary: JSON output puts rule states in Rust's internal debug format
findings.evidence: `"states": format!("{:?}", r.states)` emits a string like "[InForce, InForce, NotInForce]" rather than a structured object keyed by rule name with the 'in force'/'not in force'/'unknown' texts. A script reading `--json` would have to parse Rust's debug format. Nothing tests the JSON path.

check_origin reuses GhClient::origin_repository, which accepts only https://github.com URLs (its own test shows ssh:// returns None). An owner whose origin is [email]:o/r.git gets an error (exit 1) instead of the check. This matches the reading's 'reuse the existing helper' assumption, but parse_remote could support more URL forms.

findings.summary: Some flags are silently ignored when combined with --host-rules
findings.evidence: `--no-checkpoint` has no conflict or requires rule, so `athena check --host-rules --no-checkpoint` is accepted and the flag does nothing. `--full-replay` is already refused because it requires `--attribution`.

findings.summary: Required rules are picked by array position
findings.evidence: `rule_index < 2` and `rule_index == 2` depend on the order of the RULES array. Naming the required (branch, rule) pairs, or matching on the rule strings, would survive reordering. The report also prints non-required rules (e.g. 'main: force-push forbidden: not in force') next to the pass line, which a reader may find confusing, though the final summary line makes clear which rules count.

summary: The change does what was asked. It adds `athena check --host-rules`, which conflicts with the other check modes. The command reads the origin URL, parses owner and repo with the existing `GhClient::origin_repository` helper, and calls the existing read-only host_rules check, which makes plain `gh api <path>` GETs. It prints the per-rule report and then either an all-in-force line or one line per missing required rule. It exits 0 when every required rule is in force and 2 otherwise; a rule that cannot be read counts as not in force. I ran the athena-cli host_rules tests (3 pass), the athena-core host_rules tests (7 pass) and `check --help`, which lists `--host-rules` and its description. The tests use fixture replies. They check exit code 0 with the exact report text, exit 2 with text naming each branch and missing rule, and that every recorded call is a two-argument `api <path>` read with no flags. fmt, clippy and the full test suite passed in the CI run Athena recorded. All four changed files are on the deliverables list. Three minor problems remain: the JSON output puts rule states in Rust's internal debug format, origins over SSH are refused, and some flags are silently ignored when combined with `--host-rules`. None of them breaks a criterion.
